items.stem: Define work in a scientific context. How is it calculated when a constant force and the displacement of an object are in the same direction?
items.answer: In science, work is said to be done when a constant force acts on an object and causes it to be displaced. It is a measure of the energy transferred. When the force and displacement are in the same direction, the work done is defined as the product of the magnitude of the applied force and the displacement of the object. Mathematically, it is expressed as Work = Force Work, Energy, and Simple Machines × displacement (W = F × s). The SI unit of work is the joule (J).

items.stem: What are the two specific conditions under which the work done by a force on an object is considered zero? Give one example from daily life to support your answer.
items.answer: Work done is zero if either the displacement of the object is zero, or if the applied force is perpendicular to the direction of displacement. For example, if you push hard against a rigid, immovable wall, you may feel physically tired from muscle contractions, but the scientific work done on the wall is zero because the displacement of the wall is zero. Similarly, a person carrying a heavy box horizontally does zero work against gravity because the upward force is perpendicular to horizontal displacement.

items.stem: A student claims that a goalkeeper catching a fast-moving football does positive work on the ball because he uses a lot of energy to stop it. Do you agree? Justify your answer.
items.answer: I disagree with the student’s claim. When a goalkeeper stops a fast-moving football, the goalkeeper’s hands apply a stopping force on the ball in the outward direction. However, the ball still travels a short distance backward into the goalkeeper’s hands before coming to a complete stop. Because the applied force and the displacement of the ball are in opposite directions, the work done by the goalkeeper on the ball is negative, not positive. Positive work requires force and displacement in the same direction.

items.stem: (a) Identify in which case work is being done and in which case it is not. (b) Explain the scientific reason behind your identification.
items.answer: (a) Work is being done in case (b) where the boy pushes the wheelchair, but no work is done in case (a) where the boy pushes the wall. (b) According to the scientific definition, work requires both an applied force and a displacement of the object. In case (a), despite applying force, the wall’s displacement is zero, resulting in zero work. In case (b), the wheelchair undergoes a displacement in the same direction as the applied force, resulting in positive work being done on the wheelchair.

items.stem: Explain the concept of the work-energy theorem. How are the work done on an object and its energy connected?
items.answer: The work-energy theorem states that the work done on an object is equal to the change in its energy. When positive work is done on an object, it gains energy, which gives it the capacity to do further work or apply force to another object. For example, when a fielder throws a cricket ball, he does work on the ball, transferring energy to it. The ball gains kinetic energy, which it later uses to do work on the stumps by knocking them over.

items.stem: Define kinetic energy. How is it related to the mass and velocity of a moving object?
items.answer: Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by an object strictly due to its motion. Any moving object, such as a rolling ball or a flying bird, possesses kinetic energy. The kinetic energy of an object is directly proportional to its mass and the square of its velocity. It is mathematically expressed as K = ½ mv². This means that if the mass of the moving object increases, its kinetic energy increases. Similarly, if the object’s velocity is doubled, its kinetic energy increases by four times.

items.stem: Derive the mathematical expression for the kinetic energy of an object of mass ‘m’ moving with a velocity ‘v’, starting from rest.
items.answer: Consider an object of mass ‘m’ starting from rest (initial velocity u = 0). A constant force ‘F’ causes a displacement ‘s’, giving it a final velocity ‘v’ with constant acceleration ‘a’. Work done ,W = F × s ...(i) According to Newton’s second law, F = ma. Using the kinematic equation v² - u² = 2as, s = v² / 2a. Substituting these into the work equation gives, W = ma × (v² / 2a) = ½ mv². By the work-energy theorem, this work equals the kinetic energy.

items.stem: Draw a labelled diagram showing a person shooting an arrow using a stretched bow. Explain how potential energy converts into kinetic energy in this action.
items.answer: When the archer applies a force to pull the string, work is done to deform the bow’s shape. This work is stored as elastic potential energy in the bent limbs of the bow. When the string is released, the bow rapidly returns to its original unstretched shape. In doing so, the stored potential energy is immediately transferred to the arrow, converting entirely into kinetic energy, causing the arrow to fly forward at high speed.

items.stem: Why does the kinetic energy of a fast-moving car increase four times when the driver suddenly doubles its speed? Explain using the relevant formula.
items.answer: The kinetic energy of a moving object depends on its mass and its velocity, given by the mathematical formula K = ½ mv². The mass of the car remains constant, but the kinetic energy is directly proportional to the square of its velocity (v²). When the driver doubles the speed from ‘v’ to ‘2v’, the new kinetic energy becomes ½ m(2v)² = ½ m (4v²). Therefore, a twofold increase in velocity results in a fourfold increase in the car’s overall kinetic energy.

items.stem: Draw a diagram of a simple swinging pendulum showing its extreme and mean positions. Explain how the conservation of mechanical energy applies to its motion.
items.answer: As the pendulum moves from an extreme position (P) to the central mean position (Q), its vertical height decreases, meaning its gravitational potential energy decreases. Simultaneously, its speed increases, converting the lost potential energy into kinetic energy. At Q, kinetic energy is maximum and potential energy is minimum. As it swings toward the other extreme (R), kinetic energy converts back to potential energy. Ignoring air resistance, the sum of kinetic and potential energy (total mechanical energy) remains constant throughout.

items.stem: Compare kinetic energy and potential energy with respect to their fundamental cause and provide one distinct everyday example for each.
items.answer: Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by an object by virtue of its physical motion, whereas potential energy is the stored energy an object has due to its specific position, shape, or configuration relative to other objects. An example of kinetic energy is a fast-moving cricket ball, which can do work by knocking over wickets. An example of potential energy is water stored at a height behind a dam, which holds gravitational potential energy due to its elevated position before it falls.

items.stem: Explain the concept of gravitational potential energy. Write its mathematical expression and state the variables it depends on.
items.answer: Gravitational potential energy is the energy stored in an object due to its vertical position or height above the surface of the Earth. When work is done against gravity to lift an object to a certain height, that work is stored as gravitational potential energy. Its mathematical expression is U = mgh. This equation shows that the gravitational potential energy of an object depends directly on three factors: the object’s mass (m), the acceleration due to gravity (g), and its height (h) above the ground. items.stem: (a) What is the definition of potential energy? (b) How do you derive the expression for the gravitational potential energy of an object at a height ‘h’? (c) If a 5 kg mass is raised to a height of 10 m, what is the energy stored in it? (Take g = 10 m/s2)
items.answer: (a) Potential energy is the energy stored by an object due to its position, configuration, or deformation. (b) To derive the expression for gravitational potential energy, consider an object of mass m lying on the ground. To lift it to a height h at a constant velocity, an upward force equal to the gravitational force (mg) must be applied. The work done on the object against gravity is W = force × displacement, which gives W = mg × h = mgh. This work done is stored entirely in the object as gravitational potential energy (U), therefore, U = mgh. (c) For the numerical, given mass m = 5 kg, height h = 10 m, and acceleration due to gravity g = 10 m/s2. Substituting these given values into the derived formula: U = mgh = 5 × 10 × 10 = 500 J. The energy stored is 500 Joules.

items.stem: (a) What is meant by the power of a machine, and what is its SI unit? (b) If a water pump lifts 500 kg of water to an overhead tank at a height of 20 m in 100 seconds, what is the power of the pump? (Take g = 10 m/s2)
items.answer: (a) Power is defined as the rate at which work is done or the rate at which energy is transferred by a machine. It describes how quickly or slowly a specific amount of work is accomplished. Mathematically, average power is calculated by dividing the total work done by the time taken (P = W / t). The SI unit of power is the watt (W), where one watt is equal to one joule of work done per second. (b) In the given scenario, the work done by the pump is equal to the gravitational potential energy gained by the water. Mass (m) = 500 kg, Height (h) = 20 m, Time (t) = 100 s, g = 10 m/s2. Work done (W) = mgh = 500 × 10 × 20 = 100,000 J. Power (P) = W / t = 100,000 J / 100 s = 1000 W. The pump’s power is 1000 Watts.

items.stem: (a) What is an inclined plane, and how does it act as a simple machine? (b) What is the formula for the mechanical advantage of an inclined plane? (c) If a person pushes a 600 N box up an inclined ramp that is 3 m long and 1 m high, what is the mechanical advantage and the ideal effort required?
items.answer: (a) An inclined plane is a simple machine consisting of a flat, sloped surface that helps raise or lower heavy objects. It makes work easier by allowing a smaller effort force to move a heavy load over a greater distance, rather than lifting it vertically which requires a force equal to the object’s entire weight. (b) The mechanical advantage (MA) of an inclined plane is defined as the ratio of its length to its vertical height (MA = L / h). (c) In the given problem, the length of the ramp (L) is 3 m and its height (h) is 1 m. The load (weight of the box) is 600 N. The mechanical advantage is MA = 3 / 1 = 3. Since , MA = Load / Effort, we can rearrange this to find the ideal effort required: Effort = Load / MA. Effort = 600 N / 3 = 200 N.

items.stem: (a) What is the statement of the law of conservation of mechanical energy? (b) How do you prove that the total mechanical energy of a freely falling body of mass ‘m’ remains constant during its fall from a height ‘h’? 96. Define mechanical advantage. What is the formula to calculate it, and what does a mechanical advantage greater than 1 signify?
items.answer: Mechanical advantage is a ratio that describes how a machine changes the magnitude of the applied force to overcome a load. It is calculated using the formula: Mechanical Advantage = Load / Effort. When a simple machine has a mechanical advantage greater than 1, it means the machine acts as a force multiplier. This signifies that the machine allows a person to lift or move a heavy load by applying an effort force that is much smaller than the actual weight of the load.

items.stem: Draw a labelled diagram of a simple fixed pulley used to lift a load. Explain why it is widely used even though its mechanical advantage is only 1.
items.answer: A fixed pulley does not multiply the applied force, which is why its mechanical advantage is exactly 1; the effort equals the load. However, it is widely used because it changes the direction of the effort force. Instead of lifting a heavy load vertically upward against gravity which is awkward and strenuous a person can conveniently pull the rope downward. Pulling downward allows the person to use their own body weight to assist in applying the necessary effort, making the task practically easier.

items.stem: Why do hilly roads wind around gentle slopes rather than going straight up the mountain? Explain using the concept of inclined planes and work.
items.answer: Hilly roads are designed as winding inclined planes to make ascending the mountain easier for vehicles. If a road went straight up, it would be a very steep incline, requiring a massive engine effort to overcome gravity over a short distance. By winding around the hill, the road creates a gentle slope, significantly increasing the total distance traveled. Since the total work done (force × distance) to reach the peak remains constant, increasing the distance reduces the required effort force, making it safer and easier for vehicles.

items.stem: Describe the structure of a simple lever. Define the three main parts of a lever and explain how they interact to lift an object.
items.answer: A lever is a simple machine consisting of a rigid bar that is free to rotate around a fixed pivot point. It has three main parts: the fulcrum, which is the fixed point of rotation; the load, which is the heavy object or force that needs to be overcome; and the effort, which is the force applied by the user to move the load. By applying a small effort force at a longer distance from the fulcrum, the lever amplifies this force to lift a heavier load placed closer to the fulcrum.

items.stem: Compare Class I and Class II levers with respect to the relative positions of their fulcrum, load, and effort. Give one real-life example of each class.
items.answer: In a Class I lever, the fulcrum is positioned squarely between the applied effort and the load. A common real-life example of a Class I lever is a pair of scissors or a playground seesaw. In contrast, in a Class II lever, the load is positioned directly between the fulcrum and the applied effort. A practical everyday example of a Class II lever is a wheelbarrow or a lemon squeezer. Both types offer different ways to manipulate force and distance.

items.stem: How does a lever allow a smaller effort force to lift a much heavier load? What is the trade-off regarding the distance the effort must move? Work, Energy, and Simple Machines
items.answer: A lever allows a smaller effort force to lift a heavier load by increasing the distance between the effort and the fulcrum, known as the effort arm. According to the principle of levers, the product of effort and effort arm equals the product of load and load arm. To gain this mechanical advantage, the trade-off is distance. The end of the lever where the smaller effort is applied must move through a much greater distance to move the heavy load over a significantly smaller distance.

items.stem: What would happen if a simple machine, like a system of movable pulleys, could operate with absolutely zero friction? Discuss its efficiency and the work done.
items.answer: If a simple machine like a pulley system operated with absolutely zero friction, it would be an ideal or perfect machine. In this hypothetical scenario, no energy would be lost as thermal energy or sound due to friction. The mechanical energy would be entirely conserved, meaning the total work output of the machine would be exactly equal to the work input provided by the effort. The machine would achieve 100% efficiency, effectively converting every joule of applied work into useful work done on the load.

items.stem: Draw a simple diagram showing a heavy block being pulled up an inclined plane. If the height of the plane remains the same but its length is doubled, how does this affect the mechanical advantage?
items.answer: The mechanical advantage of an inclined plane is calculated by the ratio of its length to its height (L/h). Since the total work done remains constant, pushing an object up a slope requires applying effort over the length of the plane. If the height remains the same but the length (L) is doubled, the slope becomes much gentler. The mechanical advantage is therefore doubled, which means the required effort force to pull the heavy block up the plane is reduced to half.

items.stem: When a fast-moving truck applies its brakes and skids to a complete stop on a highway, what happens to its kinetic energy?
items.answer: When a moving truck applies its brakes and skids, it initially possesses a large amount of kinetic energy due to its motion. As the brakes lock and the tires skid against the rough road surface, a strong frictional force opposes the truck’s motion. This frictional force does negative work on the truck. The truck’s kinetic energy does not disappear but is entirely transformed into thermal energy (heat) and sound energy due to the intense friction between the tires and the road surface, eventually bringing it to rest.

items.stem: Describe the continuous energy transformations that take place in a traditional Himalayan watermill (panchakki) from the time water flows down the hill to the grinding of grain.
items.answer: In a traditional Himalayan watermill, the process begins with water stored or flowing from a high altitude, which possesses significant gravitational potential energy. As this water flows downhill through pipes or channels, its height decreases and its speed increases, converting the potential energy into kinetic energy. This fast-moving water strikes the blades of a wooden turbine or wheel at the bottom, transferring its kinetic energy to make the wheel rotate. The rotating wheel turns the grinding stone above it, using the mechanical energy to crush grains.

items.stem: What type of energy is stored in a stretched rubber band? How does the amount of stretch affect the distance a projectile attached to it will travel?
items.answer: When a rubber band is stretched, it is deformed from its original shape, and the work done by the pulling force is stored as elastic potential energy. If a small projectile is attached and the band is released, this stored potential energy quickly converts into kinetic energy. The amount of stretch directly dictates the energy stored. Therefore, pulling the rubber band further back stores a greater amount of potential energy, which translates into a higher kinetic energy and a faster, longer-distance flight for the projectile.

items.stem: (a) Based on the diagram, which part represents the effort and which part represents the load? (b) Explain why the seesaw remains balanced despite the vast difference in their weights.
items.answer: (a) The heavy adult seated on the left represents the load, while the lighter child seated on the right represents the effort applied to balance the system. (b) The seesaw balances because a lever operates on the principle that effort multiplied by effort arm equals load multiplied by load arm. The adult has a larger weight (load) but sits very close to the fulcrum (short load arm). The child has a smaller weight (effort) but sits much further away (long effort arm). These products equalize, keeping the board perfectly horizontal. LON G Answer QUESTION
